::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Unsure how to treat y in this derivative/log problem](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1568837/unsure-how-to-treat-y-in-this-derivative-log-problem), asked by [windy401](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/160580/windy401) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2015-12-10; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> Need to find the derivative of $h(y)= \ln(y^2 \cos y)$
>
> Treating it like a normal variable like an x isn't working for me, the way we used y's in earlier problems where you get a y' in there doesn't seem right, so I'm not quite sure here.
:::

If $h(y) = \ln(y^2 \cos y)=2 \ln y + \ln(\cos y)$, then
$$h'(y) = \frac{2}{y} + \frac{-\sin y}{\cos y} = \frac{2}{y} - \tan y$$

Stella is right.  In this problem, $y$ is an independent variable.  You may have worked other problems where $y$ was dependent on $x$, but this is not the case here.
